name: Adam Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the rural electric co-op out of Pinebrook. Long lines, a lot of country, a lot of trees. Most days it's outage calls, a squirrel in a transformer, a branch on a line, or changing a pole a farmer backed his trailer into. I like that nobody's standing over you out there. What I don't like is the paperwork when you get back, and the phone, they keep wanting us to use the phone for everything.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet. I live with my girlfriend Claire, she works at the pharmacy on Main Street. I fish on the weekends at the reservoir, hunt in the fall with my brother. I grew up on my uncle's dairy farm about ten miles out, so I still help him out with haying in summer. I don't do much online, never tried any of those AI things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never thought it was going to amount to much. Probably wouldn't say it online, I'm not really on there. At the shop we'd just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing, and that's fine. I like my job the way it is. I don't need a computer telling me how to fix a line I've fixed a hundred times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing I do now. Go to work, take the calls, go fishing on Saturday. Put a bit in savings every month, I've got about two months put away and I'd keep at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. Nothing to feel, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they keep wanting you to use the phone. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They gave us an app for logging jobs, and now there's talk of one that tells you which pole to check first. I just call dispatch, Linda knows the system better than any app. I'll use the app when they make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd actually want to change about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More guys, maybe. Some of these feeders are forty miles long and there's two trucks for the whole county at night. That's not a computer problem, that's a budget problem.

S0.say: I'd say I never thought it would amount to much. I'm not really online, so at the shop we'd just shrug and move on.
S0.think: It means nothing to me and that's fine, because I like my job as it is. I don't need a computer telling me how to fix a line I've fixed a hundred times.
S0.do: Keeps going to work, taking outage calls and fishing on weekends. Keeps adding a bit each month to his roughly two months of savings and uses work apps only when required.
S0.quote: I don't need a computer telling me how to fix a line I've fixed a hundred times.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is a man of few words who prefers calling Linda in dispatch to any app. He doesn't see the plateau as news at all. Like many line crews, his real complaint is staffing on long rural feeders at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office folks who should be worried, not us. Someone still has to climb the pole. That's what I'd tell my brother, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think it'd touch me much. Maybe they'd cut some of the people in the office and dispatch, which would be a shame for Linda. But out in the county, it's still me and a truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing, at first. I'd wait and see what the co-op actually does before I worried. If they made me take a training, I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sorry for the office people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You seem pretty sure the hands-on part is safe. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the poles they want robots to climb. Half of them are in a swamp or behind somebody's barn. Good luck getting a robot back there in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op told you that you had to start using new tools to keep the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it. I'm not going to quit over an app. I'd grumble, but I'd learn the minimum.

S1.say: I'd say it's the office people who should worry, not us, because someone still has to climb the pole. That's what I'd tell my brother.
S1.think: I don't think it would touch me much. They might cut office and dispatch staff, which would be hard on Linda, but out in the county it's still me and a truck.
S1.do: Waits to see what the co-op actually does before worrying about it. Takes any required training and learns the minimum, grumbling, rather than quitting over new tools.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a bit sorry for the office staff.
S1.quote: Half of them are in a swamp or behind somebody's barn. Good luck getting a robot back there in March.
S1.fieldNote: His confidence comes from the terrain: swampy, awkward rural poles he can't picture a robot reaching. He'd go along with required training but only to the minimum. His concern is for Linda in dispatch, not for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably wouldn't say much. Maybe "well, that's that." I'm not one for making speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be in real trouble. If they've got robots that can get to those swamp poles too, then what am I for? I don't have a plan B, I don't know computers, I don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra. No new rifle, no new boat motor, I'd been looking at one. I'd try to stretch the two months into four. And I'd probably go back to the farm, help my uncle for room and food if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like a pit in my stomach. I'd be up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "I don't know" a couple of times. Is there anything you'd fall back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm, I guess. My uncle always says there's work there for family. It doesn't pay, but you eat. Unless they've got robots for milking too, which, come to think of it, they already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Claire that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd be okay, even if I didn't know that. Then we'd sit down and figure out what we've got. Her job's probably safer than mine, so we might be living on hers for a while.

S2.say: I probably wouldn't say much, maybe just "well, that's that." I'm not one for making speeches about things.
S2.think: I'd be in real trouble. If robots can reach even the swamp poles, I don't know what I'm for, and I have no plan B and no wish to learn computers.
S2.do: Stops extra spending, dropping plans for a new rifle and boat motor, and tries to stretch two months of savings into four. Falls back on his uncle's farm for room and food if needed.
S2.feel: A pit in his stomach; he'd be up at night.
S2.quote: If they've got robots that can get to those swamp poles too, then what am I for?
S2.fieldNote: This is the first time Adam's flat calm breaks, and it breaks hard, because his whole confidence rested on the terrain. His fallback is family, not government, and he half-laughs that the farm already has milking robots. He'd tell Claire they'd be fine without believing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, five years is a long time, a lot can happen. Maybe it slows down. That's what I'd tell the guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's still the same problem, I'd just have longer to dread it. I don't see myself learning a new job. I'd hope they keep a few of us on to babysit the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, try to get to six months by the time it hits. I'd keep working and see what the co-op does. If they offered some kind of training to run the new machines, I'd probably take it, because what else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not as bad as the two-year one, but it'd be in the back of my head every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to save, mostly. And time to see if it's actually real or if it's like those self-driving trucks they kept saying were coming. I've been hearing about those since high school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait. What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I saw the robots actually working on our lines. Not on TV, here. Then I'd know.

S3.say: I'd tell the guys five years is a long time and a lot can happen. Maybe it slows down.
S3.think: It's the same problem, I'd just have longer to dread it. I don't see myself learning a new job, so I'd hope they keep a few of us on to watch the robots.
S3.do: Saves harder toward six months by the time it arrives and keeps working while watching what the co-op does. Takes training to run new machines if offered, because he sees no other choice.
S3.feel: Anxious, with the worry in the back of his head every day.
S3.quote: I've been hearing about those since high school.
S3.fieldNote: Adam uses the extra time mainly to save and to doubt; his reference point is self-driving trucks that never arrived. He'd only act once he saw robots on his own co-op's lines. Training is something he'd accept, not seek.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off. No point getting worked up about 2036. I'd change the subject, probably talk about fishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still in my head. Ten years is real time, but it's still the end of the job. I'd just keep hoping it doesn't happen like they say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working. Keep saving. Maybe in a few years, if it's clearly coming, look at what my uncle's doing with the farm, or something nearby. I'm not going to go back to school at thirty, that's for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Ten years is far enough I can mostly forget about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In ten years you'd be thirty-seven. Where do you picture yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, still here, maybe on the farm more. Claire and I always talked about getting a few acres out past the reservoir. That might be the plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything about your plans with Claire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might wait a bit longer to buy the land. Want to know there's money coming in first. Other than that, no.

S4.say: I'd say 2036 is a long way off and there's no point getting worked up about it. I'd probably change the subject to fishing.
S4.think: Privately it's still in my head, because ten years is real time but still the end of the job. I'd keep hoping it doesn't happen the way they say.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, and in a few years looks at his uncle's farm or nearby work if the change is clearly coming. Rules out going back to school and delays buying land with Claire until income is clearer.
S4.feel: A bit uneasy, but far enough off that he can mostly forget it.
S4.quote: I'm not going to go back to school at thirty, that's for sure.
S4.fieldNote: Distance lets Adam push it out of mind; he'd literally change the subject to fishing. His instinct is to wait, save and drift toward the farm rather than plan a new career. The plan to buy a few acres with Claire is what would quietly shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. That's the one where I'd have nowhere to go. What would help is the co-op keeping guys on to look after the machines, give us first shot, and maybe some money to tide us over. And not making me sit in a classroom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe ask the people building these robots if they've ever been out in the county at 3 a.m. in an ice storm. I'd like to hear that answer.

headlineQuote: Maybe ask the people building these robots if they've ever been out in the county at 3 a.m. in an ice storm.
portrait: Adam Dubois is a 27-year-old lineworker for the rural electric co-op in Pinebrook, a quiet man who fishes, hunts and still helps with haying on his uncle's dairy farm. He lives with Claire, who works at the pharmacy, and has about two months of savings. He has never used AI, prefers to call dispatch rather than use an app, and believes rural poles are too awkward for robots. He is calm through the mild pictures, badly shaken by AGI in two years, and with more time mostly saves, waits and drifts toward the farm rather than planning a new career.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op keeping lineworkers on to look after the machines with first shot at those jobs, some money to tide people over, and no classroom retraining.
